intro: To find clauses across hundreds of contracts on a Mac, start with Acrobat's Advanced Search on a folder of PDFs. Then log every hit, so you never search the same file twice. Apple and Microsoft's help pages do not describe a built-in tool for clause-level search across a whole contract library. The method matters as much as the software.
tldr: Run Acrobat's Advanced Search on a folder of PDFs for a first pass.
Use Word's Find only for close reading, because it works inside one open document.
Test Spotlight on one contract whose clause you already know before you trust it.
Keep a clause log with the contract, clause type, section and any date to watch.
Lazur points, guides and dictates. It does not search or index your contract folder.

blocks.text: Why finding clauses across hundreds of contracts is hard

A clause is not a file. It is a few sentences buried in one section, and the same idea can be written many ways. An indemnity clause might say indemnify, defend or hold harmless. A renewal term might sit in the main body, in a schedule, or in an email that amended it. When you search hundreds of files, you need every wording, not one exact phrase.

The labeling problem is bigger than most people expect. The CUAD dataset, built under the supervision of experienced lawyers, labels 41 types of legal clauses across 510 commercial contracts. That is a research dataset, not a law firm's files. It still shows how many clause types a careful reviewer has to track at once.

items: Different names for the same clause, such as indemnity and hold harmless.
Clauses placed in schedules, exhibits or amendments instead of the main text.
Scanned PDFs where the text is only an image, so a search cannot read it.
Files saved under vague names like Final_v3 or copy of MSA.
Contracts spread across email attachments, shared drives and old laptops.

blocks.text: What it costs when a clause is missed

The clearest number comes from outside law firms. World Commerce & Contracting reported in 2012 that poor contract management costs companies an average of 9% of annual revenue. The full report is member-only. Treat that as a company-level estimate from a 2012 summary, not a measure of lawyer hours.

Lawyer time is the other cost. The Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a median hourly wage of $76.76 for lawyers in May 2025. That figure is a rough cost anchor, not a billing rate. Multiply it by the hours spent hunting through files, and the hunt stops looking cheap.

Thomson Reuters' 2025 report says legal professionals expect AI to free up nearly 240 hours per year, up from 200 in 2024. That is a survey expectation, not a measured result for clause search. Read it as a sign of demand for faster review, not as a promise.

blocks.title: Missed dates cost more than hours
blocks.text: The worst clause misses are dates. A notice window that closes before anyone reads the renewal section can renew a contract you meant to end. Build the date check into the search, not after it.

Repetitive file work also wears people down. A study by Krill and Anker, backed by the ABA, found that 47.4% of lawyers reported high or very high work-related burnout. That study did not measure contract search. Treat it as context for why a sane workflow matters, not as proof that search causes burnout.
Why the usual Mac search tools fall short

Word's Find and Replace works inside the document that is open. Microsoft's help page describes the search box in the upper-right corner, where Word highlights every match. Press Control + H for the basic Find and Replace pane. Press Command + PERIOD to stop a search in progress. The page describes one document, not a folder of files.

Acrobat is the strongest built-in option for PDFs. Adobe's guide says to choose Edit > Advanced Search or press ⌘F. Then set Look in to a folder on your computer. Advanced Search supports AND, OR and NOT, so one search can cover several wordings. It matches words, not meaning.

Spotlight opens with ⌘ Space and finds apps, files, emails and messages as you type. Apple says it uses a local, private index on your device. I could not confirm from Apple's pages that Spotlight shows text matches inside every contract. Test it on one contract whose clause you already know.

blocks.text: Searching a folder of PDFs with Acrobat Advanced Search

This is the best first pass when your contracts are PDFs in one folder. Keep the originals in a folder you do not edit. If you need to mark up a copy, work on the copy, so the signed version stays untouched.

items: Open Acrobat, then choose Edit > Advanced Search, or press ⌘F.
Under Look in, choose the folder that holds the contracts. Acrobat also offers a PDF Portfolio or an index.
Type your first wording, such as indemnify. Add OR for each variant, such as hold harmless.
Use AND to narrow the results, such as change of control AND assignment.
Use NOT to drop boilerplate you keep seeing in every file.
Open each hit, check the section, then log it in your clause log before you move on.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Say you need every contract that lets a counterparty end the deal when ownership changes. Search for "change of control" OR "change in control" OR merger, then narrow with AND termination. Read each hit. Some will mention the phrase only in a definition, so the search gives candidates, not answers.

blocks.title: Save what you found
blocks.text: Write the file names into your clause log as you go. A search you cannot repeat is a search you will have to run again next month.
Using file names and Spotlight to narrow the set

Narrow the set before you search it. Sort contracts by counterparty and type into folders, so Acrobat scans fewer files. Spotlight helps when you remember a file name. Press ⌘ Space, type the name, and open the file from the results.

If Spotlight misses a folder you know holds contracts, check the Search Privacy list in System Settings. Apple's guide says a folder on that list is excluded from search. To fix a search problem, add the folder to the list, wait, then remove it so Spotlight reindexes it.
Build a clause log as you go

A clause log turns a one-time hunt into a record you can reuse. Each row names the contract, the clause type, where it sits and any date that matters. Keep the log in a spreadsheet, in the same folder as the contracts. Here is a simple layout.

blocks.caption: Example rows only. Enter your own clauses and dates.

blocks.text: Write the section as it appears in the contract, not as a page number. Page numbers change when someone edits the file. Add the date you last checked, so the log shows what has gone stale.
Free habits that make the next search faster

items: Name files the same way every time, such as counterparty, contract type and signing year.
Store originals in one folder, and keep drafts and markups in another.
Write a short checklist of the clauses your practice always needs, and check each file against it.
Have a colleague re-check a sample of files that were already searched, to catch misses.
Keep a running list of wordings you have seen, so the next search uses all of them.

blocks.text: If you use an AI tool to pull clauses, check its output. In the Vals Legal AI Report from February 2025, the top AI tool scored 75.1 on data extraction. The lawyer baseline scored 71.1. The test was vendor-funded, and clause location was not tested as its own task. Read it as a reason to verify, not a ranking to trust.
Mistakes people make when they search contracts

items: Searching one exact phrase and stopping when it returns nothing.
Trusting a hit without reading the section around it, which may be a definition.
Forgetting amendments, side letters and emails that change a clause.
Searching an out-of-date copy while the signed version sits in another folder.
Keeping notes in a personal app that the firm cannot find later.

blocks.text: The biggest mistake is treating search as the whole job. Search finds candidates. A lawyer still decides what the clause means and whether it matters for the client.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

For this problem, that means help with Acrobat's Advanced Search or Word's Find controls while you work. Ask Lazur to point at the Look in control, or to walk you through a search one step at a time. Hold fn to dictate a clause log entry at the cursor, so you keep your hands on the file.

Here is what Lazur does not do. It does not click buttons for you, edit files or operate other apps. It does not index a folder of contracts or search all of them in the background. Background research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, which suits public sources, not client files.

faq.question: Can Word search several contracts at once on a Mac?
faq.answer: Not from what Microsoft documents. Word's Find and Replace works inside the document that is open. For a folder of PDFs, use Acrobat's Advanced Search with Look in set to the folder. For Word files, open each one, or save copies as PDF first and search the folder.

faq.question: Does Spotlight search the text inside my contracts?
faq.answer: Spotlight finds files, emails and messages, and it keeps a local, private index on your Mac. I could not confirm from Apple's pages that it shows text matches in every contract. Test it on one file whose clause you know, then decide how much to rely on it.

faq.question: Can Acrobat search for meaning, or only exact words?
faq.answer: Acrobat Advanced Search matches words and supports AND, OR and NOT. It does not read meaning. Add each wording you expect, such as indemnify, hold harmless and defend, and read every hit before you log it.

faq.question: Can Lazur search all my contracts for a clause?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not index your folders or search files in the background. It points at controls, guides you one click at a time, answers out loud, dictates text and drafts text. You still run the search and read the contracts.

faq.question: Is it safe to show client contracts to an AI assistant?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on client data first, and some firms ban AI tools on client files. Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: How accurate are AI tools at pulling clause data?
faq.answer: In the Vals Legal AI Report from February 2025, the top tool scored 75.1 on data extraction. The lawyer baseline scored 71.1, and other tools scored lower. The test was vendor-funded and did not test clause location on its own, so verify every result against the signed text.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a macOS app for Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

costs.title: Missed notice and renewal dates
costs.text: A missed date can keep a contract running for another term, or it can close a window to object. Clause misses often show up as dates, not as wording. Set a date check for every renewal, notice and consent clause you find, so the cost of a miss stays visible.

costs.title: Lawyer hours spent hunting
costs.text: Hours add up fast when each contract is a fresh hunt. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median lawyer hourly wage at $76.76 in May 2025. That is a cost anchor, not a rate you can bill. Thomson Reuters says legal professionals expect AI to free nearly 240 hours a year, which is an expectation, not a measured saving.

costs.title: Company-wide losses from poor contract management
costs.text: World Commerce & Contracting reported in 2012 that poor contract management costs companies an average of 9% of annual revenue. That figure covers contract management in general, not clause search. Use it to justify a clause log to a partner, and cite the source with its date.

costs.title: Repeat searches and lost context
costs.text: Every time someone searches from scratch, the hunt starts again. Without a log, the next person does not know which files were checked, which were false alarms and which need a second read. The cost is duplicate work and a higher chance of a miss.

costs.title: Stress and fatigue
costs.text: Repetitive file work adds to fatigue in a profession where burnout is already common. An ABA-backed study by Krill and Anker found 47.4% of lawyers reported high or very high work-related burnout. It did not measure contract search, so treat it as context, not a direct cost of this task.

causes.title: Clauses are written in many ways
causes.text: The same obligation can appear as indemnify, defend or hold harmless. The CUAD dataset labels 41 types of legal clauses across 510 commercial contracts, which shows how many wordings and types a reviewer must track. A search built on one exact phrase will miss most of them.

causes.title: Contracts sit in too many places
causes.text: Contracts arrive as email attachments, sit in shared drives, live on old laptops and get copied into case folders. Each copy can differ from the others. A search that covers one location misses the rest. Pick one home for originals before you search.

causes.title: Amendments change clauses without changing the main file
causes.text: A side letter, an amendment or an email can change a term while the main contract stays the same. A search finds the base document, and the change lives somewhere else. Log each amendment next to the clause it changes.

causes.title: Some files do not return matches
causes.text: A scanned PDF can be a picture of a page, not text. Word's Find covers only the open document, according to Microsoft's help page. Some files may return no matches at all, so test a few early to learn which ones need a closer read.

causes.title: Mac search tools find files, not clauses
causes.text: Spotlight finds files, emails and messages. Acrobat finds words across a folder. Neither reads a contract the way a lawyer does. Apple and Microsoft's help pages do not describe a built-in clause search across a contract library, so expect to combine tools.

causes.title: Loose naming and folder habits
causes.text: Names like Final_v3 or copy of MSA hide what a file is. Folders by year or by client mix counterparties with contract types. Each vague name adds time to the hunt, and each new copy adds one more file to check.

fixes.title: Start a clause log on day one
fixes.text: Make the log before the first search, not after. Use one row per clause hit, with the contract name, clause type, section as written, any date to watch and the reviewer's initials. A log turns a one-time hunt into a record you can reuse. It costs a spreadsheet and a few minutes per file.

fixes.title: Name files the same way every time
fixes.text: Use one pattern every time, such as counterparty, contract type and signing year, in that order. Consistent names make folder searches faster and help Spotlight match file names when you are in a hurry. Rename only a copy, and log the old name so you can trace the file later.

fixes.title: Use Acrobat folder search with OR and AND
fixes.text: Search the folder once for each family of wordings. Combine variants with OR, such as indemnify OR "hold harmless" OR defend. Narrow with AND, such as "change of control" AND termination. Check which PDF app your firm has installed before you start, so you use the same tool everyone else uses.

fixes.title: Use Word Find for close reading
fixes.text: Word's Find and Replace is for reading one contract closely. Open the file, press Control + H for the basic pane, and step through the matches. Use the Navigation Pane settings for Advanced Find & Replace when you need more control. Do not rely on it to cover a folder, because Microsoft's help page does not describe that.

fixes.title: Write a clause checklist for your practice
fixes.text: List the clauses your practice always needs, such as term, renewal, notice, termination, assignment, change of control, governing law, indemnity, liability limits and confidentiality. Check every file against the list. A checklist turns a vague hunt into smaller, repeatable searches, and it makes work easier to hand to a colleague.

fixes.title: Get a second reader on a sample
fixes.text: Ask a colleague to check a sample of files that were already searched. Pick the sample at random, not the files you liked. Each miss they find becomes a new wording in your variant list. This catches the search gaps that one person keeps repeating.

fixes.title: Verify AI output against the text
fixes.text: If you use an AI tool to pull clauses, open the source section every time. The Vals report found AI tools trail lawyers on some tasks and lead on others, so no single result is safe to trust. Treat AI output as a list of candidates, and confirm each clause against the signed document before you log it.

fixes.title: Test Spotlight before you rely on it
fixes.text: Pick one contract whose clause you know. Search for a phrase from inside it, starting with ⌘ Space. If the file does not appear, add its folder to the Search Privacy list, wait, then remove it so Spotlight reindexes the folder. Apple's guide describes this fix. Do not assume a full search until you have tested it.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Pick one folder and one clause type
plan.text: Choose the folder that holds the most contracts of one type, such as supply agreements. Pick one clause to hunt first, such as auto-renewal. Write down the wording variants you expect before you search, so the first pass is deliberate.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Run the Acrobat first pass
plan.text: Open Edit > Advanced Search, set Look in to that folder, and run your variants with OR. Write the hit file names into your clause log before you open any file. Keep the originals untouched.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Close read every hit
plan.text: Open each hit, read the section around it, and check for definitions and amendments. Mark each hit as a real clause, a definition or a false alarm. Log the section as written, not as a page number.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Check every date
plan.text: Filter your log for renewal, notice and consent dates. For each one, decide the date you need to act. Ask Lazur to add a reminder to Apple Reminders by voice, or add it to Calendar yourself.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Spot check and update the wordings
plan.text: Ask a colleague to re-check a sample of this week's files. Write one line about what the search missed. Add that wording to your variant list, so next week's search starts stronger.
